name: Catholic human dignity
summary: The Vatican’s note distinguishes human intelligence from AI and places human dignity and the common good at the center of its evaluation.
illuminates: The human person is more than a set of tasks a machine can perform.
limit: This is Catholic teaching, not the position of every Christian tradition or a test of technical capability.
questions: Does delegated judgment still serve the person who bears its consequences?
Does this interaction support embodied human relationships or displace them?
Who becomes easier to overlook when efficiency defines value?
What happens when a tool is asked to provide ultimate meaning?

name: Qur’anic verification
summary: This passage warns against acting on unverified news in ways that harm others. The AI application here is an editorial question, not a ruling.
illuminates: The connection between checking information and responsibility for harm.
limit: One passage cannot represent Islamic law, diverse schools, or the whole tradition.
questions: What must be checked before acting on this answer?
Does familiarity with a voice become a substitute for verification?
Who is harmed when a claim spreads before it is checked?
What evidence distinguishes a claim about an event from an interpretation of its meaning?

name: Jewish ethical responsibility
summary: Hillel’s questions bring responsibility to oneself, responsibility beyond oneself, and the urgency of action into view.
limit: A short ethical passage does not establish a consensus Jewish position on AI.
questions: What responsibility remains mine after I delegate a task?
Does the tool make me more available to other people?
Whose interests are absent from my decision?
Does a grand forecast become a reason to postpone a responsibility I already have?

name: Action and its fruits
summary: This verse connects action with a warning against attachment to its fruits and against inaction.
illuminates: The difference between doing responsible work and making the outcome the whole measure of a life.
limit: A reading of this verse is not a summary of Hindu traditions or an AI policy.
questions: Am I attending to the quality of the action, or only its promised payoff?
What desire does this interaction repeatedly reward?
Does a promised benefit excuse the way it is pursued?
Can I act responsibly without claiming certainty about the future?

name: Impermanence and attachment
summary: The path verses include reflection on the impermanence of conditioned things.
illuminates: Attachment to an experience, a tool, or a view can itself become an object of attention.
limit: This is a selected textual lens, not an account of all Buddhist schools or a clinical claim.
questions: Am I becoming attached to an answer because it feels reassuring?
What happens when I cannot access this tool?
Which habits of attention are being cultivated?
Am I treating a changing technical system as a permanent source of security?

name: Evidence and risk
summary: The voluntary AI RMF supports incorporating trustworthiness into AI design, use, and evaluation.
illuminates: Performance needs to be evaluated in context, alongside the risks and responsibilities of use.
limit: Risk management does not settle theological claims or decide which ends a person should value.
questions: What test would show this system is unreliable for this decision?
What observed outcomes would justify the claim that it helps?
Which failures, affected people, and remedies are included in the evaluation?
What separates an observed capability from a forecast?

name: Human rights and oversight
source: UNESCO · Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
summary: The recommendation addresses proportionality, safety, privacy, participation, accountability, and oversight.
illuminates: The interests of people affected by a system, including those who did not choose to use it.
limit: An ethical recommendation is not proof of implementation or a substitute for applicable law.
questions: Can the affected person understand and challenge the decision?
What privacy and autonomy costs accompany the convenience?
Who can contest the system, and obtain a remedy?
Whose rights might be traded away in the name of an imagined future?

name: Indigenous data governance
summary: CARE foregrounds collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, and ethics in Indigenous data governance.
illuminates: Access to data is not the same thing as legitimate authority over its use.
limit: These principles do not represent every Indigenous people or authorize any particular use of community knowledge.
questions: Who has the authority to permit this use of knowledge?
Does a personalized tool respect the communities behind its data?
Who controls the data, receives the benefits, and bears the costs?
Who gets to shape the future being proposed?
